title: Cloudflare's default block on mixed-use AI crawlers takes effect
subtitle: As of September 15, 2026, ad-supported sites on Cloudflare block AI training and agent crawlers by default unless publishers opt in.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Cloudflare's July-announced policy — blocking 'mixed-use' AI crawlers by default on any Cloudflare-fronted page that carries ads — went live on September 15, 2026. The default flip applies to new customers, newly added sites on existing accounts, and all existing free-plan sites; enterprise customers keep their prior settings unless they opt in. Site owners can override in either direction, but the shipped default now says 'blocked' rather than 'allowed' for crawlers that mix search indexing with training and agent traffic.

The rule turns on Cloudflare's classification of a crawler's declared purpose. A bot that fetches a page only for a search index is treated differently from one that also feeds a training set or drives a live AI agent — and the AI vendors have until this date to separate those bots or accept the block. The company paired the flip with an evolution of its Pay Per Crawl experiment into Pay Per Use, where publishers get paid when their content is cited in an AI answer rather than merely when a bot fetches the page, with Ceramic.ai and You.com as launch partners.

Cloudflare fronts a very large share of the open web, so this is not a policy paper — it is a network default change that AI companies have to work around every day. Combined with the wave of publisher lawsuits and the OpenAI/Anthropic content licensing deals from 2025-2026, the direction is unmistakable: unlabeled crawling of the ad-supported web is being priced in, not just called out.

Takeaway for learners: the web your models trained on and the web they can crawl tomorrow are diverging. If you're building an AI product or research pipeline that assumes free scrape access to news and reference sites, budget for data licensing or restrict to explicitly open sources — the reachable open web is narrowing, one CDN policy at a time.
